title: Suraqa's horse
hook: Suraqa, chasing for the reward, sinks in the sand and turns back (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asma tore her waistband to tie the food bags. Your line was: two belts. What did you tie shut with what you already had? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

A price on two heads. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Suraqa ibn Malik tells this story himself. Messengers from Quraysh came to his tribe, offering a reward to anyone who killed or captured the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or Abu Bakr. Suraqa was sitting with his people when a man walked up and said: I just saw figures moving along the coast. I think it's them. Suraqa knew it was. And he said out loud: no, that's just some travelers we know. He wanted the reward for himself. Today: Suraqa's horse.
screen: `A PRICE ON TWO HEADS.` → `FIGURES ON THE COAST.` → `NO, JUST SOME TRAVELERS.`

segments.voice: Suraqa waits a little, goes home, and quietly sends his horse out behind a hill. He takes his spear and rides. As he nears them, his horse stumbles and throws him. In his own telling, he draws lots with divining arrows, the custom of the time, and the answer comes out against him: don't harm them. He rides anyway. He gets close. Close enough, he says, to hear the Prophet reciting. And he notices something: the Prophet does not look back, while Abu Bakr keeps turning around to look. Then the ground gives way. His horse's forelegs sink into the earth up to the knees, and he is thrown. He urges the horse up. It can barely pull its legs out, and when it stands, dust rises from the tracks of its legs like smoke. He draws lots again, and again the answer is the one he doesn't want. At last Suraqa does the thing a hunter doesn't do. He calls out to the men he is chasing and asks for safety. They stop. He tells them everything: the reward, what people are planning. He offers them food and supplies. They take nothing. They ask him only one thing, in effect: keep our matter hidden. And he asks for a written promise of safety, which Amir ibn Fuhayra, Abu Bakr's freed man, writes for him on a piece of leather. The shape of the story matters. It is not about outrunning him. The fugitives never run faster. The chaser is the one who is stopped, by the ground and by his own lots, until he gives up the chase himself. The ground did what the travelers couldn't. And the man who set out to sell them ends up guarding their secret, holding their promise in his hand.
screen: `HE RIDES ANYWAY.` · `CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR HIM RECITE.` · `THE HORSE SINKS TO THE KNEES.` · `THE HUNTER ASKS FOR SAFETY.` · then, large: `KEEP OUR MATTER HIDDEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: let a chase go. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Think of something you're chasing right now. Maybe a win, an argument, a person's approval, a reward with someone else's name on it. Notice how it feels to keep riding after it. Then picture your horse's legs slowing in soft sand. You don't have to fight it. Let it stop. Ask: what if I called out instead of charging? If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you which chases to let go. Rest in the stillness. The bell holds the time.
Suraqa's horse. In Bukhari, its legs sink into the ground as Suraqa chases the Prophet for the reward, until he gives up the chase and asks for safety. Today's word.
Your line: the sand held him back. Today, when you notice yourself pushing hard after something, let the ground slow you once, and see what happens when you stop. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims retell Suraqa ibn Malik's chase from his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari as part of the hijrah story.

original.note: Arabic: the name Suraqa, of Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, who tells the story.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chase scene from the hijrah.
what it means: the fugitives never outran him; the hunter was stopped until he chose to stop.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 (Suraqa's account: the reward, the figures on the coast, the divining arrows, the horse sinking, the request for safety, the writing on leather)

notes: Bukhari 3906 cited from memory; confirm number and details (divining arrows, sinking to the knees, Amir ibn Fuhayra writing on leather).
The index hook says he sinks 'three times'; the script does not give a count, since the hadith as recalled describes repeated stumbling and sinking without that exact number. Confirm.
Script says the sinking happens 'again' after he pulls the horse free; confirm against the hadith's sequence.
'Abu Bakr's freed man' for Amir ibn Fuhayra; confirm.
howItsDone says he later became a Muslim (commonly reported, at the conquest of Mecca); not stated in the script. Confirm.
The popular story of the bracelets of Kisra is left out; it is not in Bukhari 3906.

Audit pass: restored the first stumble that comes before the first casting of lots in Bukhari 3906 (as recalled), so 'he rides anyway' has its cause; dust now rises 'from the tracks of its legs' rather than 'behind it'.

Editor pass: the teach had the horse sinking a second time and a 'draw lots, sink, fall' loop; Bukhari 3906 as recalled has one sinking, the horse struggling free with dust rising like smoke, then a second casting of lots before he calls out, so the sequence was corrected; cut 'he later became a Muslim' from howItsDone (not in the cited text); varied the 'look at' opener.
